clue.text: Sweet product of iPod sales?

explanation.surface: A dessert dreamed up as the by-product of selling music players.
explanation.walkthrough: Apple makes the iPod, and a firm's turnover is its sales revenue, so the second reading is the company's takings; the first is the fruit pastry.
explanation.definitionFit: A pastry dessert of folded fruit-filled dough is a sweet, and the takings of the firm behind the iPod are its revenue figure.

clue.text: Any road rather than north, if you don't care

definitions.note: a phrase describing a state of indifference, standing for the noun

indicators.note: one thing used rather than another means a letter in the word is swapped out for a substitute

parts.note: N is the compass abbreviation for north
a path is a road or track

explanation.surface: Someone who couldn't care less will take any route except the northern one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rather than north' means replace the N of ANY with PATH (road), giving A-PATH-Y.
explanation.definitionFit: Indifference, or a lack of interest and concern, is exactly the state of not caring.

clue.text: Treated like a dog, cocked leg?

parts.note: to cock something, like an ear or a leg, is to put it up
in cricket the leg side is also called the on side

explanation.surface: A dog lifting its leg, and being badly treated for it.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the leg side of the field is also called the on side, so 'leg' gives ON.
explanation.definitionFit: Being exploited or imposed upon is being treated with contempt, as one might mistreat a dog.

clue.text: When they clash, you'll 'ear either or I go!

definitions.text: When they clash, you'll 'ear either or I go!

parts.words: When they clash, you'll 'ear either or I go!
parts.note: the row of two big personalities is 'either he or I go', and with the h dropped, as the apostrophe in 'ear signals, 'e goes sounds like the plural word wanted

explanation.surface: Two people in a feud, one shouting an ultimatum in a dropped-aitch accent.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe in 'ear tells you to drop the H, so 'he goes' becomes ''e goes', which sounds like the answer, the things that clash in such a row.
explanation.definitionFit: Inflated senses of self-importance are what collide in a quarrel where each says the other must leave.

clue.text: Ill fitting lingerie around two articles held apart

indicators.note: the two copies are kept apart, each one placed at a different point inside the garment word
the garment word goes around the first of the two articles, enclosing it

parts.note: lingerie is women's underwear
the definite article is the word the; two of them are needed
the second definite article, the

explanation.surface: Badly fitting underwear wrapped around a couple of items that are kept apart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'around' puts one THE inside UNDERWEAR; 'held apart' says the second THE goes in at another point, giving UNDER-THE-WEA-THE-R.
explanation.definitionFit: Feeling slightly unwell or poorly is the idiom's meaning.

clue.text: Sex offender not attached to church

parts.note: non is a prefix meaning not
CE is the abbreviation for Church of England

explanation.surface: A sex offender who has no connection to any church.
explanation.walkthrough: NONCE is British slang for a sex offender, especially a child abuser.
explanation.definitionFit: British prison slang for a child molester or similar criminal.

clue.text: Pill's uplifting, animative contents

indicators.note: in a down clue, uplifting means the letters are read upwards, so backwards
the contents of a word are the letters inside it, without its first and last

explanation.surface: A tablet whose ingredients lift the mood and liven you up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'contents' gives NIMATIV, the inside of 'animative'; 'uplifting' turns it upwards in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A supplement is often taken as a tablet, so the pill stands for the nutrient it supplies.

clue.text: Polo's run over pet

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece over another means it is written above, so first

parts.note: a run of good luck is a roll, as in being on a roll
to pet amorously is to neck

explanation.surface: Someone's pet getting run over by the car called a Polo.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Polo' suggests the VW car or the mint, but it is the polo neck, a high-collared sweater.
explanation.definitionFit: A polo neck is a sweater with a high turned-over collar, the same garment under another name.

clue.text: Big Mac, say, an oxymoron?

parts.note: a burger is quick-service eating, and the clue points out that to go without eating is also to abstain, so the phrase is self-contradictory

explanation.surface: A burger chain's signature sandwich described as a contradiction in terms.
explanation.walkthrough: To fast is to go without eating, so the term for quick meals pairs a word for abstaining with a word for eating.
explanation.definitionFit: A Big Mac is a classic quickly served takeaway burger.

clue.text: Stingy one let off after tax deducted

indicators.note: the jumbled letters come after the tax word in the answer

parts.note: pay with tax deducted is net pay

indicators.note: off signals that the letters are spoiled or rearranged

explanation.surface: A mean person allowed off once the tax has been taken.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stingy' reads as mean, but here it means having a sting, like the plant. 'off' rearranges LET into TLE.
explanation.definitionFit: The weed with hairs that sting the skin is a plant that stings.

clue.text: Persuade MPs with joint

parts.note: the hip is a joint of the body

explanation.surface: Getting members of parliament on side with a joint of something.
explanation.walkthrough: A party whip is the official who makes MPs vote along party lines; whipping is that persuading.
explanation.definitionFit: In parliament, party officials enforce voting discipline among members, an act of urging them into line.

clue.text: Milton Keynes' economic rival?

parts.note: read not as the English town but as an economist called Milton who was the rival of John Maynard Keynes

explanation.surface: A new town in England and its competitor for business.
explanation.walkthrough: Milton Keynes is an English new town, but split apart it is Milton, the monetarist economist, opposing Keynes, the economist.
explanation.definitionFit: The Chicago monetarist Milton argued against Keynesian economic theory.

clue.text: Objections over smoking end

indicators.note: over in a down clue signals the word is turned upside down, so read backwards

parts.note: buts are objections, as in no ifs or buts

explanation.surface: Protests against smoking, ending a habit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' reverses BUTS (objections) in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: The butt left after a cigarette is smoked is its remnant.

clue.text: Potter might be flying after this grass

definitions.text: Potter might be flying after this

explanation.surface: Harry Potter on a broomstick chasing a tell-tale.
explanation.walkthrough: In Harry Potter's sport of Quidditch the seeker flies after the golden ball with wings; 'grass' is slang for an informer.
explanation.definitionFit: The winged golden ball in Quidditch is chased by the boy wizard, and an informer who tells on others is a grass.

clue.text: Such might be applied to bruised area governor after loss of key state

definitions.text: Such might be applied to bruised area

indicators.note: loss of means the musical key letter is dropped from the governor's name

parts.note: Arnie, Arnold Schwarzenegger, was governor of California
E is a musical key
CA is the abbreviation for California

explanation.surface: Ointment applied to a bruise belonging to a governor after a state was lost.
explanation.walkthrough: Arnold Schwarzenegger, Arnie, was Governor of California; dropping E (a key) leaves ARNI, then add CA, the state.
explanation.definitionFit: A herbal remedy from a mountain plant, used as a cream to soothe bruises.

clue.text: Ray's turning out awkward

indicators.note: turning out signals that the letters are rearranged into a new form

parts.note: the letters of Ray's, the S included

explanation.surface: Ray proves to be difficult company.
explanation.walkthrough: ARSY is British slang for contrary or bad-tempered.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang for being difficult, uncooperative or contrary.

clue.text: Where one's absent from work, perhaps, may dread being rumbled

definitions.text: Where one's absent from work, perhaps

indicators.note: being rumbled, found out or disturbed, signals the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A worker who skips the office fears being caught out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'absent from work' looks like truancy, but it means being lost in thought; 'being rumbled' rearranges MAY DREAD.
explanation.definitionFit: A reverie is a state of mind where one is absent in thought though present in body.

clue.text: Take a sharp turn on secondary road in European capital

parts.note: to zag is to change direction sharply, as in zig and zag
re means on, regarding
a B road is a secondary road in Britain

explanation.surface: Driving a twisting minor road into a European capital.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain, B roads are secondary roads, below A roads.
explanation.definitionFit: The capital city of Croatia.

clue.text: Bow, oar and stern of it all found at sea

definitions.text: Bow, oar and stern of it all found at sea

indicators.note: at sea means confused, so the letters are in disarray
the stern is the back of a boat, so the last letter of the word

explanation.surface: A list of a small boat's parts, all out on the water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stern of it' gives T, the last letter; 'at sea' mixes it with BOW and OAR.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue describes a small vessel propelled by oars, with its bow and stern out on the water.

clue.text: Saucy Japanese type would swing both ways?

definitions.text: Saucy Japanese type would swing both ways?

parts.words: Saucy Japanese type would swing both ways?
parts.note: saucy means a condiment, and someone who swings both ways is bisexual

explanation.surface: A flirtatious Japanese person who is bisexual.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saucy' sounds risqué but means a sauce-like condiment; the pungent green paste served with sushi, split up, reads 'was a bi'.
explanation.definitionFit: A hot green horseradish paste served as a condiment with Japanese food.

clue.text: God, he's drunk — give us a hand, do you hear?

indicators.note: do you hear signals that a phrase is to be heard and spelt differently

parts.note: to back us is to support us, give us a hand

explanation.surface: Someone drunk calls on God and asks for help.
explanation.walkthrough: The Roman god of wine; 'give us a hand' is 'back us', which sounds like his name.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman deity of wine and revelry, often shown intoxicated.

clue.text: God, he's gorgeous, ace Spanish bloke is

parts.note: A is the abbreviation for ace in cards
Don is a Spanish title for a gentleman

explanation.surface: Someone swooning over a handsome Spaniard.
explanation.walkthrough: The beautiful youth of Greek myth, loved by Aphrodite.
explanation.definitionFit: The handsome youth of Greek myth whose name now means an attractive man.

clue.text: Reduced tonnage that's taken from net

parts.note: to be down is to be reduced or lowered
a load is the weight or tonnage carried

explanation.surface: Lower cargo taken from a fishing net.
explanation.walkthrough: 'net' suggests fishing, but it is the internet.
explanation.definitionFit: A file copied from the internet onto a computer.

clue.text: Express doubt after hair cut by temp

indicators.note: the doubtful word comes after the shortened hair word in the answer
cut means the hair word is shortened, losing its last letter

parts.note: a lock is a tress of hair
um is a sound expressing hesitation or doubt

explanation.surface: Someone expresses doubt after a temporary stylist cuts their hair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cut' docks LOCK to LOC, and 'after' places UM behind it.
explanation.definitionFit: A stand-in doctor or cleric covering temporarily for another is a stopgap worker.

clue.text: It's said top player's to give up

indicators.note: it's said signals that a word is heard and spelt differently

parts.note: a seed is a top-ranked player in a tennis tournament

explanation.surface: A top player is reported to have resigned.
explanation.walkthrough: In tennis the best players are seeded; 'It's said' turns SEED into its soundalike.
explanation.definitionFit: To surrender or yield something, such as territory.

clue.text: Dot's partner Mark

explanation.surface: A woman called Dot and her boyfriend Mark.
explanation.walkthrough: In Morse code the dot is paired with the dash; a dash is also a punctuation mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Morse code pairs the short dot with a long signal, and the horizontal line in punctuation is a mark.

clue.text: Chore I discharged like a lion

indicators.note: discharged signals the letters are set off or released into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone finishing a chore with great courage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'discharged' rearranges CHORE and I.
explanation.definitionFit: Brave and bold, as a lion is said to be.

clue.text: E.g. voodooists roast chickens

parts.note: to roast is to heat
hens are chickens

explanation.surface: Voodoo practitioners cooking chickens.
explanation.walkthrough: Voodoo involves animal sacrifice, which is why chickens fit the picture.
explanation.definitionFit: Followers of a non-mainstream religion such as voodoo were called pagans by outsiders.

clue.text: Shape-shifting change atomises me internally

indicators.note: internally means one piece is placed inside the other
change signals the letters of atomises are rearranged

parts.note: me is the setter, Morph

explanation.surface: A shape-shifter's change splits the speaker into atoms from within.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter is Morph, so 'me' is MORPH, set inside ETAMOSIS, a rearrangement of ATOMISES.
explanation.definitionFit: A transformation of form, as a caterpillar turns into a butterfly.
